scenes.synopsis: the dragon's silence — no letters for two nights; the quiet, priced. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Morning, and Letitia comes to breakfast with the overnight intelligence.)*
> "Nothing, darling." The hawk's eyes are puzzled. "No letters for two nights. Honoria says the dragon's desk is —" she lowers her voice — "quiet. She's not writing."
> "She's planning."
> "Or she's —" Letitia stops. "Tired? Honoria said tired. Do dragons get tired, darling?"
> *(Rose considers the question with her chocolate. Two nights without letters. The refusals have stalled at fourteen. The acceptances climb daily. The dragon's silence could be exhaustion, or regrouping, or the worst possibility: a new weapon, not yet deployed.)*
> "We don't relax," Rose says. "Tired dragons are still dragons. Double the calls."
> "Double the calls, darling." Letitia reaches for the address books. "I do love a war."

scenes.synopsis: the historian's parallel — Harrow on the guest-list wars of the past; perspective. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Harrow finds her in the gallery, and walks with her among the portraits.)*
> "The '78 assembly." He nods at a Ravencroft. "Your great-grandmother's ball. The same war — letters, debts, absence. The same dragon, different scales." A dry look. "She won. They always do, miss — the hosts. Not because they're better. Because they're *there*. The house is there. The supper is there. Absence is a weapon that only works until the night itself."
> "And then?"
> "And then the room is either full or it isn't, and everyone sees which." He stops before the Park-drawn-whole. "History's lesson, miss: Drummond can keep people away from the invitation. She can't keep them away from the night. Nights have their own gravity."
> *(They walk on. The portraits watch — the whole long argument of blood, framed and dusted — and the historian's parallel settles over the campaign like dust settling after a charge: the hosts win, because they're there.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Hartwell rose, budding — the gardener's report; the bloom, on schedule. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walled garden, morning: the gardener's report, delivered with soil on his hands.)*
> "The bud's coloring, Miss Hartwell." He shows her — the green tightness giving way to the first blush. "A week. Ten days at most. It'll open for the ball, miss —" he grins — "roses have their own intelligence about these things."
> "And the housewarming's flowers?"
> "Cutting starts in five days. Every stem Hartwell-grown." He straightens. "The ton'll walk through our garden, miss. Literally. I've planned the route — the terrace urns, the ballroom's great vases, the supper room's low bowls. They'll breathe us in."
> *(She bends to the bud — the blush, the certainty — and the legacy, literal and living, is on schedule. Ten days to the first bloom of the Hartwell rose. Ten days to the ball. The garden keeps its own calendar, and the calendar is holding.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry mends the war-room's map; service, in small things. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He finds her in the war-room at midnight — the map torn at the fold, the campaign's casualty — and produces a needle and thread from his dispatch case.)*
> "You carry sewing kit in a dispatch case, Major?"
> "I carry everything in a dispatch case." He mends the fold with small, exact stitches — the soldier's neatness. "A map is an instrument. Instruments get maintained." He ties off. "There."
> *(She looks at the mended fold — the small exact stitches — and at the man who carries sewing kits in dispatch cases, and the war-room's midnight feels suddenly, absurdly, like the safest place in England.)*
> "Thank you, Henry."
> "It was a small thing." He packs the kit. "I am —" the smallest smile — "practicing."

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at midnight — two hundred chairs; the war, being won. (Turns: 7)

scenes.synopsis: the final issue's shape — Bell on what the paper will print; the last word, planned. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell comes with the final issue's shape in her head — the proprietor, planning the last judgment.)*
> "The ball gets the front page." She states it flatly. "The verdict — unsparing and just — waits for the final assembly. But the ball —" the notebook opens — "the ball gets the reporting: who came, who didn't, what the dragon wore, what the gown —" a look — "what Élise's gown *did*. The town will read it Monday and argue about it for a year."
> "And the verdict?"
> "The verdict is written." The notebook closes. "I've been writing it for ten seasons, Miss Hartwell. The final assembly just gives me the last paragraph." She moves to the door. "One proprietor to another: whatever the ball costs you, it doesn't cost you the paper. The paper was never yours to lose."
> *(Rose watches her go — the straight back, the shut notebook — and the final issue's shape settles: the ball, reported; the verdict, waiting; the last word, on the paper's own terms.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ballroom, dressed — Hartwell-grown flowers; the great room, in bloom. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ballroom, Thursday: the flowers going in — the great vases filled with Hartwell-grown blooms, the gardeners on ladders, the room transforming.)*
> *(She stands in the doorway and watches the room bloom — the terrace urns' sisters inside now, the supper room's low bowls waiting their turn, the whole great room filling with the garden's own. The ton will walk through Hartwell's flowers and breathe the Park. The gardener's plan, executed.)*
> *(The ballroom is forty paces of polished possibility, and the possibility is being dressed in flowers. In three days it holds the ton. The wanting is still there — the honest wanting — and the flowers don't diminish it. They decorate it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the final tasting — the supper, approved; the Hartwell rose ice, attempted. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:

> "The rose ice, Miss Hartwell." The confectioner presents it with ceremony. "Rosewater from the garden's roses — not the Hartwell rose, not yet, but its sisters. Taste."
> *(She tastes: the cold, the floral, the exact. It is the garden, frozen — the Park's summer, kept.)*
> "Approved." She signs the diagrams. "All of it. The supper is —" she looks at the cook, the confectioner, Mrs. Quick — "the supper is the house's argument, and the argument is won."
> "The house's argument, miss." The cook is serene. "We've been making it for ten seasons. Saturday we serve it."

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry checks the moonlight drive; the ball's first impression, secured. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He walks the moonlight drive with her — the lanterns steady now, the limes hung with light, the full moon two days away.)*
> "Steady." He tests a chain. "Every one. The drive's the ball's first impression —" the soldier's certainty — "and the first impression is the lanterns, the moon, and the house lit like —" he stops.
> "Like what, Henry?"
> "Like something that intends to be seen." He looks at the house — the windows lit, the Park whole. "It does, Rose. Intend it, I mean. I've watched you build it for —" another stop — "for a long time. Saturday the ton sees it. I wanted —" the smallest smile — "I wanted the drive to be worthy."
> *(They walk back in the dusk. The devotion in the evening is the week's steadiest preparation — the gift of attention, on purpose, in lanterns.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at noon — 380 chairs; the room, full. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Noon, and the arithmetic: three hundred and eighty chairs — the final week's fifth day, the last acceptances in, the silences written off as cowards.)*
> "Three hundred and eighty, darling." Letitia sets down the pen. "The ballroom holds four hundred. We have three hundred and eighty. The fourteen refusals —" she draws the line — "the fourteen are Drummond's, and they can keep each other company."
> *(Rose does the sums with the noon on the list. Three hundred and eighty. The visible win/lose, won: the ballroom will be full — not perfectly, but fully enough that the fullness is the fact. An empty ballroom is public humiliation. A full one is the verdict. The verdict is in.)*
> "The dragon's fourteen can have their evening," Rose says. "We'll have ours."
> "Ours, darling." Letitia closes the book. "Ours is better."

scenes.synopsis: the dragon, in London — her preparations, reported; the purple gown, finished. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria's last report before the ball — the dragon's preparations, complete.)*
> "The purple's finished." Honoria stands in the morning room, dry as dust. "She tried it on yesterday. She looked —" a pause — "she looked like herself. The dragon, in full plumage." A longer pause. "She asked me what I thought. I told her the truth — that acknowledgment becomes her. She —" Honoria stops — "she almost smiled, Rose. Almost."
> "And the fourteen?"
> "The fourteen are hers. She won't release them — it would look like retreat." The dry voice softens, just slightly. "But she's coming, Rose. In purple. For acknowledgment. Whatever Saturday costs her —" a look — "she's paying it beautifully."
> *(Rose sits with the report: the purple, finished; the fourteen, kept; the dragon, coming beautifully. The war's end has a shape now — and the shape is purple.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE RECEIVING (how Rose receives Drummond at the ball: at the door herself, with Augusta, or among the guests). The dragon comes; decide the receiving. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room: the receiving, planned — Drummond's arrival is the ball's true first moment, and the manner of it will be read by every guest. Augusta's spectacles are at the angle of war; Letitia's pen is poised.)*
> "At the door yourself," Augusta says, "is honor — and courage. With me beside you is the line — the Ravencrofts, receiving together. Among the guests —" the rarest smile — "is equality. Let her find you among your people, as one of them."
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The receiving:*
- **At the door, herself** — *honor, and courage.* Rose receives Drummond at the ballroom's doors, alone. (Consequence: the courage is absolute and the town sees it — but alone at the door is alone, and dragons notice solitude.)
- **With Augusta beside her** — *the line, receiving.* The Dowager stands with her granddaughter; the Ravencrofts receive together. (Consequence: the line is honored and the dragon faces two generations — but the night becomes the family's night, not Rose's.)
- **Among the guests, as equals** — *equality, offered.* Rose lets Drummond find her among her people, one host among the company. (Consequence: the equality is the message — but messages get missed, and the dragon may read it as evasion.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: honor, lineage, or equality. The dragon will come. The receiving is hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the quartermaster's joy — Letitia, at the war's end; the aunt, herself. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia in the war-room at dusk — the maps retired, the lists closed, the quartermaster with nothing left to quartermaster — and the strangest expression on the hawk's face: peace.)*
> "It's done, darling." She sits among the retired maps. "The war's over. We won." A pause. "I don't know what to do with my hands."
> "Rest them, Aunt."
> "Rest." She looks at her hands — the quartermaster's hands, steady through ten seasons. "Do you remember the first war-room, darling? The libel war. The maps. You, pricing names like ribbons." She laughs, suddenly. "We were so young."
> "We were."
> "And now —" she gestures at the finished house around them — "now the wars are over, and the house is finished, and I —" the voice does something uncharacteristic — "I'm proud, darling. Of you. Of us. Of the maps."
> *(Rose takes the quartermaster's hands — the steady hands — and the war-room holds its dusk. The aunt, herself: funny without trying, formidable without announcing it, cracking only toward love.)*

> *(The first dance ends. The leader taps his stand. The second begins. She stays for three dances, hidden in the doorway, and the wanting is there — the honest wanting — dressed now in music. Saturday the room holds the ton. Tonight it holds the rehearsal. Both are beautiful.)*

> *(Letitia's words at the announcement: the moon is a guest too, and she'll want the good candles. The good candles are lit. The moon is invited. The drive waits for its guest.)*

> *(The Park is dark beyond the window — the lake, the garden, the wall — and the Hartwell rose's bud is out there in the dark, blushing toward its opening. Two days. The bloom and the ball, together. The garden keeps its calendar. So does she.)*

> "How brilliantly, Aunt?"
> "Very, darling." The hawk's eyes shine. "The town has decided. The war's over. What remains is —" she gestures — "the brilliance. Which, I hardly need to tell you, is our department."
> *(Rose takes the letters. The town's verdict, in advance: the ballroom will be full. The visible win/lose, won before the night. What remains is the night itself — and the dragon, in purple, coming beautifully.)*

> *(Rose looks at the gown — the house, rendered in silk — and the fitting begins: the ivory, the embroidery, the fall of the skirt. It fits the way finished things fit: exactly.)*
> "Élise." Rose meets the girl's eyes in the glass. "The modiste's girl is the ton's dressmaker now. After Saturday, everyone will know it."
> "After Saturday," Élise says, "I can sleep." A grin, sudden and young. "After Saturday, Miss Hartwell, I am going to sleep for a week."

> "For Saturday." Augusta holds them up. "They were my mother's. They'll be —" the spectacles lower — "they'll be yours after, I suppose. Everything is yours after, child. The plate. The pearls. The house." A pause. "I am —" the rarest stop — "I am glad it's you."
> *(Rose kneels — actually kneels — and lets Augusta fasten the pearls around her throat. The weight is familiar. The meaning is new: continuity, worn; the line, honored; the Dowager's whole philosophy of tenderness, in a clasp.)*
> "Grandmama —"
> "Hush, child." The shaky hands, exact. "Saturday you wear the house. Tonight you wear the pearls. Both suit you."

> *(She goes to the walled garden in her dressing gown, Letitia and Augusta behind her, and the Hartwell rose has opened in the dawn — the first bloom, the legacy literal and living: the petals the color of the Park's stone at noon blushing to rose, the form perfect, the scent — she bends — the scent like nothing she has ever smelled, like the garden's whole ten seasons in one flower.)*
> "Oh." Letitia's voice is small. "Oh, darling."
> *(Augusta touches the bloom with one finger, gently. The gardener stands with his cap in his hands. Rose looks at the first bloom of the Hartwell rose — her legacy, bred across the seasons, opened for the ball — and the wanting is there, and the joy is there, and they are the same thing.)*
> "Cut it," she says softly. "Carefully. It's for Saturday."

> "Thank you, Mrs. Quick."
> "Miss Hartwell." The housekeeper's eyes shine, just slightly. "Ten years. And Saturday —" she stops — "Saturday they see it. All of it. What we kept."
> *(Rose takes the housekeeper's hands — the keys, the work, the decade — and the two hosts stand together in the hall: the mistress, and the keeper.)*

scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria's last intelligence — the dragon's carriage, ordered for Saturday.)*
> "The traveling carriage." Honoria reports dryly. "The purple gown packed. She leaves London at noon Saturday —" a pause — "she wants the entrance, Rose. The full one. The town watching." A longer pause. "She's bringing no party. Just herself. And —" the dry voice drops — "and me. She asked me to come with her. I said yes."

She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the keeping the Gazette watches annually is the keeping that's real.* — remembered: *the lesson: the keeping the Gazette watches annually is the keeping that's real.*
